title: From shared understanding to shared context · hancrafted
description: Why AI speeds up every station but not the result, how to tell static from dynamic context, how to spot context that goes bad, and how to let an AI interview you in rounds of questions to build high-signal context, then move it into a fresh chat.

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI Every product translates intent, so the result was always decided by how precise and accurate the requirement was. Both Precise Accurate Neither

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Value was always translation A product, a service or a lecture: each translates what a person wanted into something that solves the actual problem. The hard part is deciding what to build, a hypothesis from experience, not a measurement. 01 · What a person wanted The customer “I want to get to work without arriving sweaty.” One intent. 02 · What it was translated into Product E-bike Service Fitting Lecture Riding class Three translations.

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Defining and building Every effort splits into defining what to make and building it. AI speeds up building and can assist defining, only as far as it can guess what is in your head. 01 Defining Deciding what to make. AI can assist by asking. How far is your commute? Hills, or flat? 12 km, one big hill. “…as long as AI can’t read our minds.” 02 Building Making it. AI speeds it up a great deal. Frame Assemble Test ride More documents per hour at every station. Clients can’t state it up front: they find out what they want by trying versions 48% of 228 companies name incomplete or hidden requirements as their top problem; rework eats 40–50% of effort

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Precision and accuracy Precise: someone else could build it without a single question. Accurate: the result matches the intent and solves the actual problem. You need both. Tight Loose Precise, off target Work order Road racer · frame M · carbon · no mudguards At the bench: The wrong bike, built perfectly. Precise and accurate Work order Commuter e-bike · frame M · 500 Wh · mudguards · rack At the bench: The right bike, no questions. Neither Work order A nice bike, quickly. At the bench: Wrong, and full of questions. Accurate, scattered Work order Something for the commute, with a motor? At the bench: Right in the end, after a dozen questions. Off the intent On the intent Up: precision , how few questions the sheet leaves open Right: accuracy , whether it hits what the rider wanted Precise but wrong is the costly one: a missing requirement does not stop the line, it ships the wrong bike ( ) . How much that costs depends on the job ( ) .
Context is the requirement Context engineering: deciding what the AI sees, the way requirements decide what a team builds. Context window Static Dynamic

Context is the requirement (1/6) Page 1 of 6 What the AI actually sees The AI reads the window, and only the window: if you did not put it there, it does not exist. Context is the requirement (2/6) Page 2 of 6 Context engineering is requirements engineering for agents Google’s definition: context engineering is “the practice of providing AI agents with rich, structured information about your codebase, architecture, conventions, and intent.” Read as a requirement Codebase → the materials you already have Architecture → how the parts fit together Conventions → the house rules Intent → the goal Customer wants a city bike to ride to work, by Friday Same four outcomes as the dartboard Precise and accurate Context window “City bike, 54 cm frame, 7-speed hub, black, ready Friday.” Nothing to ask, nothing to guess. Precise, not accurate Context window “Road bike, 58 cm carbon frame, 22 speeds, ready Friday.” Clear, but the customer wanted a city bike. Accurate, not precise Context window “A comfortable bike for getting to work.” Right idea, ten questions left. Neither Context window “Something sporty, you know what I mean.” Vague and off target. Anthropic: aim for “the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens” that maximise the chance of the outcome you want ( ) . A parallel researchers propose ( ) ; unlike a spec, the window is a budget that changes while the agent works ( ) .

Context is the requirement (3/6) Page 3 of 6 Static and dynamic context Static is set up before the shift, dynamic arrives during it: both land on the same bench. 07:00 · Before the shift Static The pinned instruction sheet Memory files The standing rules System prompt The first work order Initial prompt 10:30 · During the shift Dynamic Parts fetched from the storeroom Retrieval A call to a supplier Web search The folder of the current job Project folder

Context is the requirement (4/6) Page 4 of 6 You run the bench You decide what lands on the bench and where the work is heading; the AI works with what you hand it. You AI worker On the bench: the work order, sheet version 3, four wrenches Held back: sheet version 1, the catalogue of every model Your job What lands on the bench Brief it like a new colleague on day one. Where the work is heading Steer when it drifts. Not your job How the worker does it inside. More is not safer 98.7% of one rule followed, alone 85.0% when 19 rules come at once gpt-4o; context files that repeat what the agent can find did not help either.

Context is the requirement (5/6) Page 5 of 6 Context rot at the bench A fuller bench can be a worse bench: four messes, set up before the shift or arriving during it. Names after Drew Breunig and IBM A wrong fact stuck in poisoning Too much history distraction Too many similar tools confusion Two instructions that disagree clash Static set up before the shift A wrong fact stuck in · poisoning A wrong screw size on the instruction sheet Too much history · distraction A binder of every bike model, when you build one Too many similar tools · confusion Fifty near-identical wrenches Two instructions that disagree · clash Old and new sheets both pinned up Dynamic arrives during the shift A wrong fact stuck in · poisoning A mislabelled box of screws Too much history · distraction Colleagues dropping by with questions Too many similar tools · confusion Ten crates of similar parts Two instructions that disagree · clash “Rush it” against “check every piece”

Context is the requirement (6/6) Page 6 of 6 Keeping the bench clean One cleanup per mess, and sometimes the cleanest fix is a clean bench. Four fixes, paired as in the IBM Technology video Other fixes exist too A wrong fact stuck in Validate Check the sheet against a real bike Too much history Compact Replace the binder with a one-page summary Too many similar tools Curate Keep only the wrenches the job needs Two instructions that disagree Prune Pull the old sheets down The cleanest fix Start at a clean bench: open a fresh chat and bring only the result, not the whole history. Long chat, leftovers and all Old chat 128K of 200K · 64% Fresh chat with the result Fresh chat 38K of 200K · 19%

Creating context for agents (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Meta prompting A separate session writes the context for you: the AI asks, you answer, and the line gets one clean work order. Planning office · separate chat What must be ready before the spring rush? Every rental bike serviced and 40 repair slots bookable. Who books the slots, and how? The front desk, by phone and walk-in. You only answer. No prompt to write from scratch. You answer better than you write Stays in the office: questions, half-ideas, drafts Fresh chat only the work order crosses The line · bike bench Work order · Spring service week Goal Rental fleet serviced, 40 slots open Who Front desk books, two mechanics Must Brakes and tyres on every bike Done when Calendar full by 1 March Written from your answers The AI worker starts from one page, not the whole conversation.

Creating context for agents (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Grill-me Matt Pocock’s grill-me skill: the AI asks a round of questions at a time, you answer, and after the last round it writes the spec: a one-page work order. Spring service week for the bike workshop The AI asks · you answer Round 1 · the goal Who is the week for: regulars or new riders? What must be ready before the spring rush? What would make the week a success? 1. Regulars first. 2. Every rental bike serviced. 3. 40 repair slots booked. Round 2 · the limits Who books the slots, and how? Which bikes are out of scope? 1. Front desk, by phone and walk-in. 2. E-bikes, they go to the partner shop. Round 3 · done when “Calendar full by 1 March.” in rounds, not one by one No gaps left. Writing the spec. Spec · Spring service week For Regulars first Must Every rental bike serviced Booked by Front desk, phone and walk-in Out E-bikes Done when 40 slots, calendar full by 1 March First page on a clean bench

Creating context for agents (3/3) Page 3 of 3 BRIEF The five moves from the freelancer Episode, and today's session runs all five. Freelancer · AI · Day 1 Callback: Onboard AI every time B Break it down Today: the line, each station, and the requirement it needs R Requirements first Today: context is the requirement, so it comes before the work I Interview with AI Today: the grill, in rounds of questions E Evaluate each step Today: read the spec before you trust it F Fresh chat Today: carry the spec into a new chat, not the long one

A thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

What the customer really wanted Why the line gets out of balance DORA's 2025 report overview says AI's primary role is as an amplifier, magnifying an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses, and that the greatest returns come from a focus on the organizational system rather than the tools. It is an overview page; the report text was not read 1 . Sources (1) DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 (overview page) ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev

What happens with AI Measured: the load moves to review On teams with high AI adoption, developers completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, while review time rose 91% and pull requests grew 154%; the report finds no significant company-level gain 1 . Sources (1) Faros AI, The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025 (23 July 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) faros.ai Engineers say the same Google engineers report that the time saved in creating is re-spent on auditing and verifying, and DORA reads this as work moving from authors to reviewers 1 . Sources (1) DORA, Balancing AI tensions ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev What is measured and what is inferred The shift to review is measured; the shift to specification is an inference from it, because no source shows unclear specifications limiting AI-sped output. It is correlational, vendor and self-reported data about software teams 1 . Sources (1) Faros AI, The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025 (23 July 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) faros.ai

Speed the whole line can carry Returns come from the system DORA's overview reports that the greatest returns from AI come from a strategic focus on the underlying organizational system, not the tools. This is an overview page, so treat it as a pointer 1 . Sources (1) DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 (overview page) ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev
Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI No speaker notes for this Slide.

Value was always translation The hard part is the concept Brooks argues the hard part of building software is deciding what to build, the conceptual construct, and not the labor of representing it in code; an error in the concept cripples the result and is hardest to rectify later 1 . Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) cgl.ucsf.edu How strong the evidence is this is one author's argument from experience, written in 1986 about human-built software. No source compares requirements and execution on the same projects, and that it holds when an AI builds is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) cgl.ucsf.edu

Defining and building Clients cannot state it up front Brooks holds that clients do not know what they want and cannot specify it completely and correctly before they have tried versions of the product, so refining requirements iteratively is what builders do most for them 1 . Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) cgl.ucsf.edu Practitioners name it too in a survey of 228 companies, incomplete or hidden requirements were the most cited requirements problem (48%), and avoidable rework is estimated at 40 to 50 percent of project effort, though the 100x late-fix rule and the CHAOS failure rates are disputed 1 . Sources (1) Why do unclear requirements lead to rework and failed projects? (earlier research file) ( opens in a new tab ) github.com

Precision and accuracy Missing requirements show up as wrong output in 55 historic aerospace software incidents, 85% produced wrong output instead of stopping, only 16% were errors of traditional programming, and 40% came from absent code, meaning missing requirements or unanticipated situations 1 . Sources (1) Prokop, Historical Aerospace Software Errors Categorized to Influence Fault Tolerance ( opens in a new tab ) ntrs.nasa.gov Limits the 40% mixes missing requirements with unanticipated situations, the categories were assigned in hindsight, and the author doubts that more requirements would have averted many of these errors 1 . A survey of specifications found that how much quality matters depends on the project 2 . Sources (2) Prokop, Historical Aerospace Software Errors Categorized to Influence Fault Tolerance ( opens in a new tab ) ntrs.nasa.gov Mund, Femmer, Méndez Fernández, Eckhardt, Does Quality of Requirements Specifications matter? Combined Results of Two Empirical Studies ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org
Context is the requirement No speaker notes for this Slide.

What the AI actually sees The window has an attention budget Anthropic says recall decreases as the number of tokens in the window increases, so context has diminishing marginal returns and an attention budget 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Context engineering is requirements engineering for agents Google’s definition Three Google authors define context engineering as “the practice of providing AI agents with rich, structured information about your codebase, architecture, conventions, and intent”, and list six kinds of context: instructions, knowledge, memory, examples, tools and guardrails. It is a practitioner whitepaper, not a study: it frames the term and does not test the parallel to requirements 1 . Sources (1) Osmani, Saboo, Kartakis (Google), The New SDLC With Vibe Coding: From ad-hoc prompting to Agentic Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com The definition Anthropic defines context engineering as curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference, guided by "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" that maximise the chance of the desired outcome 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Input quality tracks output quality in a randomized experiment with 30 novices, training in requirement-oriented prompting beat conventional prompt-engineering training (20% against 1% gains), and the authors report input-requirement quality correlates with output quality. It is a small trip-advisor chatbot study, not coding agents 1 . Sources (1) Ma, Peng, Yang, Shen, Koedinger, Wu, What Should We Engineer in Prompts? Training Humans in Requirement-Driven LLM Use ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org A proposal, not a finding researchers draw the parallel explicitly, but no source measured it; the sentence that both disciplines share a job is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Chen, Wang, Sun, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Promptware Engineering: Software Engineering for Prompt-Enabled Systems ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Where the parallel stops a requirements document gains from completeness while a context window is a finite budget that can lose from it, and context changes during a run instead of being signed off once 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Static and dynamic context Dynamic means loaded at run time agents keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths and links and load data into context at run time using tools, instead of loading everything up front 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

You run the bench More is not safer stating all requirements at once lowered compliance (98.7% for one requirement alone against 85.0% for gpt-4o with 19) 1 , and repository context files that restated discoverable information did not generally improve coding-agent success 2 . Sources (2) content-library research, Why do explicit written requirements reduce the variation in LLM output? ( opens in a new tab ) github.com Gloaguen, Mündler-Sasahara, Müller, Raychev, Vechev, Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents? (v3, 2026-09-29) ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Context rot Length alone does part of the damage output quality falls as the window fills, even with perfect retrieval 1 . Sources (1) content-library research, Why does a language model's output quality drop as its context window fills? ( opens in a new tab ) github.com The four names Drew Breunig named context poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash in June 2025: poisoning is an error that gets saved and reused, distraction a long history that steers the model, confusion superfluous material such as surplus tools, clash conflicting material in the window 1 . Sources (1) Drew Breunig, How Long Contexts Fail ( opens in a new tab ) dbreunig.com Credit and limit the IBM Technology video presents the same four. The taxonomy is a practitioner blog post and a failure can fit more than one mode 1 . Sources (1) IBM Technology, Context Engineering for AI Agents: 4 Failure Modes to Avoid ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Numbers for confusion and clash on the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard every model does worse with more than one tool, a quantized Llama 3.1 8b failed with 46 tools and succeeded with 19; piecemeal prompts cut scores by 39% on average 1 . Sources (1) Drew Breunig, How Long Contexts Fail ( opens in a new tab ) dbreunig.com

Keeping the bench clean The video's framing the IBM Technology video pairs each mode with one fix: validate, compact, curate, prune. Its closing line says all four fixes work by throwing something away 1 . Sources (1) IBM Technology, Context Engineering for AI Agents: 4 Failure Modes to Avoid ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Breunig lists other fixes his companion post names six: RAG, tool loadout, context quarantine, pruning, summarization and offloading. Picking fewer than 30 tools improved selection accuracy up to threefold 1 . Sources (1) Drew Breunig, How to Fix Your Context ( opens in a new tab ) dbreunig.com One fix per mode is a simplification compaction can launder a bad fact into a clean summary, so it does not repair poisoning; that a fresh window is the thread behind compact and prune is inference, and Anthropic warns overly aggressive compaction loses subtle but critical context 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com
Creating context for agents No speaker notes for this Slide.

Meta prompting Users answer better than they write when a model elicits preferences with open-ended questions, the user's answers are often more informative than prompts they wrote unaided, and users report it takes less effort 1 . Sources (1) Li et al., Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Prompts generated from requirements REprompt builds a multi-agent prompt optimiser from requirements-engineering principles; the abstract reports effective optimisation without numbers, and it is an early preprint 1 . Sources (1) Shi, Sun, Chen, Wu, Chen, Jin, Liu, REprompt: Prompt Generation for Intelligent Software Development Guided by Requirements Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Grill-me Where grill-me comes from grill-me is a skill Matt Pocock published in his open collection of agent skills, "Skills for Real Engineers" 1 . He presents the collection's end-to-end coding workflow in a video 2 . Sources (2) Matt Pocock, mattpocock/skills: Skills for Real Engineers (GitHub) ( opens in a new tab ) github.com mattpocock/skills: A complete AI Coding workflow, end-to-end (YouTube) ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Asking beats guessing, on unclear tasks on an underspecified variant of SWE-Bench Verified, agents that interacted with the user to fill missing information improved by up to 74% over non-interactive ones; that is a maximum, from simulated users, and models struggled to tell which tasks need a question 1 . Sources (1) Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Rounds are inferred the research backs asking clarifying questions before the task; "in rounds" is an inference. Separately, scores fell 39% on average when an instruction arrived over several turns, which measures piecemeal instructions and not clarifying questions 1 . Sources (1) Laban et al., LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

BRIEF Why a fresh chat Anthropic describes compaction as summarising the contents and starting a new context window with the summary, warns that overly aggressive compaction can lose subtle but critical context, and recommends sub-agents with clean windows that return a condensed summary 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:33 Imagine your organization as a line AI doesn't build the right swing for you, but it can build the wrong one ten times faster. Imagine your own organization as a factory line, with documents moving from one work centre to the next, a request here, a design there, a finished result at the end. You already know this picture, because everyone in this room has lived the tire swing cartoon, where each station built its own version of what the customer asked for. 0:33 – 0:58 Where this is going Before we start, here is the route. First we give every station on that line an AI and watch what happens. Then we look at what you hand the agent, because that decides the result. And last, you will see how an AI interview builds that handover for you, so you do not have to write it alone.

What the customer really wanted 0:00 – 0:15 The Hook That is the line from a moment ago: ten wrong swings, built faster. Keep it in mind, because the rest of this Episode is about why it is true and what you do about it. 0:15 – 0:35 Cartoon to balanced line Now picture the cartoon turning into a real factory line. Input comes in at a constant rate, every station keeps pace with the next, the output is steady and the quality is high. If this was how your organization worked, you would not need this Episode. 0:35 – 0:58 Reality But you know it does not work like that, because you have seen what happens when every station is pushed to go faster. Bottlenecks form, documents queue up in front of one station while the next one sits idle. So look at the line you work in and ask yourself: which station is yours?

What happens with AI 0:00 – 0:19 Every station faster So now give every station AI. Each one runs faster, which sounds like good news, but the line was only ever as fast as its slowest station, and that station cannot keep up with what arrives. You can see this in the market right now. 0:19 – 0:43 Moving bottleneck For a long time the slow part was making the thing in the first place, because a person can only make so much in a day, and that pace set the speed of everything after it. AI takes that limit away. The cost did not vanish, it moved to the next station, and it compounds there.

Speed the whole line can carry 0:00 – 0:30 One fast station is not the goal Picture the same line once more, but this time running at a higher speed and still in balance. Queues stay short and every work centre keeps pace with its neighbour. That is the goal: a sustainable increase in what the whole organization gets done, not one very fast station. Now zoom into one station: the bike bench. Keep an eye on this one station; we come back to it. 0:30 – 0:47 Bridge So what makes every station keep pace? Whatever arrives at the first station. If that is unclear, everything downstream builds the wrong thing faster. That arrival is the requirement, which raises the obvious question: what makes a requirement a good one?

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI 0:00 – 0:19 A new pain Think of the last time you got back exactly what you asked for, and it was still wrong. Nobody was lazy and nothing was broken. The building went fine, so the failure sat somewhere else, and that is the pain this Section is about. 0:19 – 0:30 Where the Section goes We take three steps. First what value actually is, then where it splits into two halves, and then what makes a requirement a good one.

Value was always translation 0:00 – 0:17 Every effort is a translation Whatever you make, a product, a service or a lecture, you are doing the same thing: you translate what a human wanted into something that solves the actual problem. The product is only the last form of that intent. 0:17 – 0:53 A translation layer Think of a restaurant guest who had to walk into the kitchen and cook from the raw ingredients. The menu and the waiter are the translation. Software works the same way: if your customer had to give orders straight to the storeroom where the data lives, in the language of that storeroom, they would not need the screens you built for them. The translation is the work. And this is my hypothesis, not a measured result: the translation is the hard part, not the typing.

Defining and building 0:00 – 0:17 Two halves Every effort splits into two halves, defining what to make and building it. AI speeds up building a great deal, and it can also assist with defining, but only as far as it can guess what is in your head. 0:17 – 0:35 Foreshadow Remember that last thought, because it comes back. Defining is exactly where the AI can help, by asking you questions the way a good interviewer would. That has a name, meta prompting, and we get to it in the last Section.

Precision and accuracy 0:00 – 0:10 Precision Start with precision. A document is precise when someone else could execute it without asking you a single question. Nothing is left to guess. 0:10 – 0:33 Accuracy Accuracy is a different thing: the result matches what you intended and solves the actual problem. Picture a dartboard: precision is darts landing close together, accuracy is darts landing on the bull. A document can be precise and not accurate, and then you have the ten wrong swings, built faster and with great care. 0:33 – 0:50 Art, not a science Now, honesty about the craft. Writing a good requirement is an art, not a science. You only know whether it was precise and accurate after you have tried it, and that is why this Section sits where it does.

Context is the requirement 0:00 – 0:18 The claim So here is the claim, and I want you to treat it as a claim: context engineering is requirements engineering for agents. What you hand the agent decides the result, in the same way a requirement decides the result for a human team. 0:18 – 0:32 The route The route has four stops. First what the AI sees, then the two kinds of context, static and dynamic, then how it goes wrong, and finally how to keep it clean.

What the AI actually sees 0:00 – 0:18 Callback If you saw the context window Episode, you have met the context window before. Everything the AI works from is what sits in the window, nothing more and nothing less, and that window is a bar that fills up with every turn. 0:18 – 0:34 Not your mind The AI cannot read your mind.
